                                               TOTAL 3-CLOSURE FOR PROJECTIVE SPECIAL LINEAR
                                                                  GROUPS


                                                          TING GONG, YONG YANG, AND MICHAEL RUOFAN ZENG
arXiv:2608.17878v1 [math.GR] 18 Aug 2026




                                                    Abstract. A finite group is totally 3-closed if every faithful permutation rep-
                                                    resentation of it is 3-closed. We study this property for the finite simple pro-
                                                    jective special linear groups. We prove that PSL2 (q) is totally 3-closed if and
                                                    only if q ≥ 7 is prime, and that PSL3 (q) is totally 3-closed if and only if either
                                                    q = 3, or q is prime and q ≡ 2 (mod 3). We further prove that PSL4 (q) is
                                                    never totally 3-closed and that PSLn (q) is not totally 3-closed whenever n ≥ 5
                                                    and q > 2. Within the family PSLn (q), only the groups PSLn (2) with n ≥ 5
                                                    remain unresolved. In particular, this answers Problem 20.2 of the Kourovka
                                                    Notebook affirmatively.




                                                                                   1. Introduction
                                               Let G ≤ Sym(Ω) and let k ≥ 1. The k-closure G(k),Ω is the largest subgroup
                                           of Sym(Ω) having the same orbits as G on Ωk . The group G is k-closed on Ω if
                                           G(k),Ω = G. This property depends on the permutation representation. A finite
                                           abstract group G is totally k-closed if every faithful action of G on a finite set is k-
                                           closed. The least such k is called the closure number of G. The notion of k-closure
                                           goes back to Wielandt [24], while total closure was introduced and developed more
                                           recently in [10, 14].
                                               The case k = 2 has been studied extensively. Abdollahi and Arezoomand classi-
                                           fied the finite nilpotent totally 2-closed groups [1], and Abdollahi, Arezoomand, and
                                           Tracey proved that the same classification holds among all finite solvable groups
                                           [2]. Among the finite nonabelian simple groups, Arezoomand, Iranmanesh, Praeger,
                                           and Tracey proved that exactly six are totally 2-closed:
                                                                  J1 ,      J3 ,      J4 ,       Ly,      Th,        M.
                                           In particular, all six are sporadic, and no finite simple group of Lie type is totally
                                           2-closed [5].
                                              This led to Problem 20.2 of the Kourovka Notebook [19, Problem 20.2]:
                                                   Are there any nonabelian simple groups of Lie type which are totally
                                                   3-closed?
                                           Freedman, Giudici, and Praeger placed this question in the broader study of closure
                                           numbers of finite simple groups. They proved that the closure number of An is
                                           n − 1, established uniform upper bounds for the remaining families, and posed
                                           further questions on the closure numbers of finite simple classical groups [14].

                                             Date: August 3, 2026.
                                             2020 Mathematics Subject Classification. Primary 20B25; Secondary 20D06.
                                             Key words and phrases. k-closure, totally 3-closed group, projective special linear group, per-
                                           mutation group, base size.
                                                                                             1
2              TING GONG, YONG YANG, AND MICHAEL RUOFAN ZENG


  We answer Problem 20.2 affirmatively and determine total 3-closedness through-
out the family of projective special linear groups, apart from one remaining infinite
family.

Theorem 1.1. Let G = PSLn (q) be a finite nonabelian simple group. Then the
following hold.
    (1) If n = 2, then G is totally 3-closed if and only if q ≥ 7 is a prime.
    (2) If n = 3, then G is totally 3-closed if and only if either q = 3, or q is a
        prime with q ≡ 2 (mod 3).
    (3) If n = 4, then G is not totally 3-closed for any q.
    (4) If n ≥ 5 and q > 2, then G is not totally 3-closed.

Remark 1.2. Thus, within the family PSLn (q), the classification of total 3-closedness
remains open only when n ≥ 5 and q = 2. Finite nonabelian simple groups of other
Lie types are not considered in this paper.

   Now we describe our approach. Simplicity gives an effective reduction from
arbitrary faithful actions to coset actions. Every nonsingleton orbit of a nonabelian
simple group is faithful, and we show that total 3-closedness can be tested on
diagonal actions on unions G/H ⊔ G/K for pairs of proper subgroups H, K < G.
This two-orbit criterion is the starting point for all of our positive results.
   Most coset actions are handled by base size. An action with a base of size at
most two is 3-closed, and such an action also governs its union with any other
transitive 3-closed action. We therefore reduce the positive cases to the relatively
small collection of subgroups whose coset actions do not have a base of size two.
   For PSL2 (p), Dickson’s subgroup classification reduces the problem to torus
normalizers, exceptional subgroups, and subgroups of a Borel subgroup. The first
two types are handled by base-size estimates. The Borel subgroups give scalar-fiber
actions above P1 (Fp ), whose 3-closures are determined by the projective quotient
and by determinant classes on the fibers. The remaining small primes are treated
using the Fano plane, the unique 2-(11, 5, 2) biplane, Paley graphs and tournaments,
and the Perkel graph.
   The proof for PSL3 (p) has a similar structure. Nonparabolic maximal subgroups
are treated using the subgroup classification and explicit trivial-intersection conju-
gates. Subgroups of point and line parabolics require a separate argument. Their
coset actions admit projective quotients, and mixed triple orbits recover equality or
incidence in PG(2, p). This forces the actions on different projective fibers to arise
from one element of the group. The case PSL3 (3) is handled separately using its
maximal-subgroup structure and one exhaustive GAP computation.
   The negative results come from local matching. On projective points, PGLn (q)
and PSLn (q) have the same orbits on ordered triples, and field automorphisms
preserve these orbits. This gives the semilinear obstruction whenever q is a proper
prime power or gcd(n, q −1) > 1. For n ≥ 4 and q > 2, we use the action on nonzero
vectors modulo the center of SLn (q). Every element of the corresponding general
linear quotient can be matched on any ordered k-tuple with k < n by an element
of the special linear quotient. Finally, the exceptional isomorphism PSL4 (2) ∼  = A8
gives the remaining negative case in dimension four.
   The paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we establish the general reduction
and base-size lemmas. In Section 3, we treat PSL2 (q). In Section 4, we prove the
            TOTAL 3-CLOSURE FOR PROJECTIVE SPECIAL LINEAR GROUPS                           3


classification for PSL3 (q). In Section 5, we establish the semilinear and central-
vector obstructions and prove Theorem 1.1.

                      2. Definitions and immediate results
   We first record the general facts used in the positive classifications. Throughout
the paper, all groups and all sets acted on are finite, actions are on the right, and
αg denotes the image of a point α under a group element g. All coset actions are
denoted by G/H. Only the associated transitive G-set and its point stabilizer are
used.
Definition 2.1. Let Ω be a finite set and let G ≤ Sym(Ω). The 3-closure of G on Ω,
denoted by G(3),Ω , consists of all σ ∈ Sym(Ω) such that, for every (α1 , α2 , α3 ) ∈ Ω3 ,
there exists g ∈ G, depending on the triple, with
                               (α1σ , α2σ , α3σ ) = (α1g , α2g , α3g ).
The action of G on Ω is 3-closed if G(3),Ω = G. A finite group G is totally 3-closed
if every faithful action of G on a finite set is 3-closed.
Proposition 2.2. Let S be a finite nonabelian simple group. Then S is totally
3-closed if and only if, for every pair of proper subgroups H, K < S, with repetition
allowed, the diagonal action of S on S/H ⊔ S/K is 3-closed.
Proof. The forward implication is immediate. Indeed, for every proper subgroup
H < S, the kernel of the action of S on S/H is the core of H in S. Since S is simple,
this kernel is trivial. Thus every action appearing in the statement is faithful.
   Conversely, let Ω be a faithful finite S-set and let σ ∈ S (3),Ω . By [14, Lemma 2.1],
applying the definition to the constant triple (α, α, α) shows that ασ ∈ αS for every
α ∈ Ω. Hence σ preserves every S-orbit.
   Every nonsingleton orbit is faithful, since the kernel of the action on such an
orbit is a proper normal subgroup of S. Let Ω1 , . . . , Ωr be the nonsingleton orbits.
Since the action on Ω is faithful, we have r ≥ 1.
   Suppose first that r ≥ 2. For each j ≥ 2, we have that σ|Ω1 ⊔Ωj ∈ S (3),Ω1 ⊔Ωj
by [14, Lemma 2.2]. Since Ω1 ∼      = S/H1 and Ωj ∼     = S/Hj for proper subgroups
H1 , Hj < S, the hypothesis implies that this restriction is induced by some sj ∈ S.
For j, k ≥ 2, the elements sj and sk induce the same permutation on Ω1 . Since the
action on Ω1 is faithful, we have sj = sk . Their common value induces σ on every
nonsingleton orbit.
   Suppose now that r = 1. By [14, Lemma 2.2], σ|Ω1 ∈ S (3),Ω1 . Consider the
diagonal action of S on Ω1 × {1, 2}, where S acts trivially on {1, 2}. Define σ         b ∈
Sym(Ω1 × {1, 2}) by (α, i)σb = (ασ , i). For any triple ((α1 , i1 ), (α2 , i2 ), (α3 , i3 )),
there exists s ∈ S such that
                               (α1σ , α2σ , α3σ ) = (α1s , α2s , α3s )
by [14, Lemma 2.1]. Since S fixes the second coordinate, the same element s agrees
with σ
     b on the original triple. Hence σb ∈ S (3),Ω1 ×{1,2} . Writing Ω1 ∼
                                                                       = S/H for some
proper subgroup H < S, this action is equivalent to the action on S/H ⊔ S/H.
By hypothesis, it is 3-closed. Thus σb is induced by an element of S, and the same
element induces σ on Ω1 .
   Finally, since σ preserves every S-orbit, it fixes every singleton orbit pointwise.
Thus σ ∈ S, and S is totally 3-closed.                                              □
4              TING GONG, YONG YANG, AND MICHAEL RUOFAN ZENG


   A base for a faithful action of G on Ω is a tuple of points of Ω whose pointwise
stabilizer in G is trivial. The base size of the action is the least length of a base.
Lemma 2.3. Let G act faithfully on Ω. If the action has base size at most two,
then it is 3-closed.
Proof. Let b be the base size of the action. If b = 2, then G(3),Ω = G by [14,
Lemma 3.2].
   If b = 1, then G(2),Ω = G by [14, Lemma 3.2]. Since G ≤ G(3),Ω ≤ G(2),Ω , it
follows that G(3),Ω = G.                                                     □
Proposition 2.4. Let S be a finite group, and let X and Y be faithful transitive
S-sets whose actions are 3-closed. Suppose that the action on X has base size at
most two. Then the diagonal action of S on X ⊔ Y is 3-closed.
Proof. Let σ ∈ S (3),X⊔Y . Constant triples show that σ preserves both X and Y
by [14, Lemma 2.1]. Moreover, σ|X ∈ S (3),X and σ|Y ∈ S (3),Y by [14, Lemma 2.2].
Since both actions are 3-closed, the restrictions of σ to X and Y are induced by
elements of S.
   Choose a base (a, b) for the action on X, allowing a = b when the action has a
one-point base. After composing σ with an element of S, we may assume that σ
fixes X pointwise.
   Let y ∈ Y . By [14, Lemma 2.1], there exists s ∈ S such that
                              (aσ , bσ , y σ ) = (as , bs , y s ).
Since σ fixes X pointwise, we have s ∈ Sa,b = 1. Hence y σ = y. Thus σ fixes both
X and Y pointwise after normalization, and the original permutation σ is induced
by an element of S. Therefore the action on X ⊔ Y is 3-closed.                 □
Proposition 2.5. Let S be a finite nonabelian simple group, and let H, K < S.
Suppose that the coset actions on S/H and S/K are 3-closed. If S ̸= HK, then
the diagonal action of S on S/H ⊔ S/K is 3-closed.
Proof. Set X = S/H and Y = S/K. Since H and K are proper and S is simple,
both coset actions are faithful. By hypothesis, both are 3-closed.
   Let x ∈ X and y ∈ Y have stabilizers Sx = H and Sy = K. Since H and K
are proper, H is not transitive on X and K is not transitive on Y . Moreover, H
is transitive on Y if and only if S = HK, and K is transitive on X if and only
if S = KH. Since S = HK if and only if S = KH, the hypothesis implies that
neither of these actions is transitive.
   Thus the hypotheses of [14, Lemma 2.3] are satisfied, and the diagonal action on
X ⊔ Y is 3-closed.                                                                □

                         3. The PSL2 (q) classification
   In this section, we prove that G = PSL2 (q) is totally 3-closed if and only if q ≥ 7
is prime.
3.1. Prime powers and large primes. We first eliminate the proper prime pow-
ers.
Proposition 3.1. Let q = pf ≥ 4 with f > 1. Then the natural action of G =
PSL2 (q) on Ω = P1 (Fq ) is not 3-closed.
            TOTAL 3-CLOSURE FOR PROJECTIVE SPECIAL LINEAR GROUPS                            5


Proof. Suppose first that q is odd. For an ordered triple T = (x1 , x2 , x3 ) of distinct
points, choose nonzero representatives vi ∈ F2q and set

                ∆(T ) = det(v1 , v2 ) det(v2 , v3 ) det(v3 , v1 )   mod (F×  2
                                                                          q ) .

This is independent of the representatives, and for A ∈ GL2 (q),
                                [∆(AT )] = [det(A)][∆(T )].
The group PGL2 (q) is sharply 3-transitive on Ω, while G has index 2 in PGL2 (q)
and is 2-transitive [12, p. 245]. Hence the square class of ∆(T ) distinguishes the
two G-orbits on ordered triples of distinct points. Moreover, any two triples with
at most two distinct entries lie in the same G-orbit whenever the same coordinates
are equal.
   Consider the Frobenius permutation
                                   ϕ : [u : v] 7−→ [up : v p ].
It preserves all equalities among the coordinates of a triple and satisfies ∆(T ϕ ) =
∆(T )p . Since p is odd, ϕ preserves square classes. Thus ϕ ∈ G(3),Ω . However, ϕ
fixes 0, 1, and ∞, so any element of PGL2 (q) inducing ϕ would be the identity.
Since f > 1, ϕ is nontrivial, and hence ϕ ∈
                                          / G.
   Suppose now that q is even. Then G = PGL2 (q), and G acts sharply 3-
transitively on Ω [12, p. 245]. Hence two triples lie in the same G-orbit if and
only if the same coordinates are equal. The same holds for Sym(Ω), so
                                   G(3),Ω = Sym(Ω) > G.
Therefore the natural action is not 3-closed.                                              □

   Next, we eliminate a small case.
Proposition 3.2. The group PSL2 (5) is not totally 3-closed.
Proof. Using PSL2 (5) ∼  = A5 , consider the natural action of A5 on five points. This
action is 3-transitive [12, Section 2.9]. Since |A5 | = 5 · 4 · 3, it is sharply 3-transitive.
Thus A5 and S5 have the same orbits on ordered triples, and hence
                                         (3)
                                       A5 = S5 > A5 .
Therefore PSL2 (5) is not totally 3-closed.                                                □

   We next prove that PSL2 (p) is totally 3-closed for every prime p ≥ 17 with p ̸=
19. Together with the preceding results, this leaves the four cases p = 7, 11, 13, 19
in the PSL2 family.
   For the remainder of this subsection, let p ≥ 17 be prime, put G = PSL2 (p) and
m = (p − 1)/2, and let U ∼= Cp be a Sylow p-subgroup of G. The Borel subgroup
NG (U ) has the form U ⋊ Cm , and for each d | m we write Hd = U ⋊ Cd for the
unique subgroup of NG (U ) containing U with |Hd /U | = d.
Lemma 3.3. Every proper subgroup of G is contained in one of the following:
     (i) the normalizer of a split or nonsplit torus;
    (ii) an exceptional subgroup isomorphic to A4 , S4 , or A5 ;
   (iii) a conjugate of Hd for some d | m.
6               TING GONG, YONG YANG, AND MICHAEL RUOFAN ZENG


Proof. By Dickson’s classification, every proper subgroup of G is contained in a
torus normalizer, a Borel subgroup, an exceptional subgroup, or a proper subfield
subgroup [16, Theorem A.1]. See also [18, Lemma 2.1]. Since p is prime, no proper
subfield subgroup occurs.
   A Borel subgroup has the form U : Cm . If L ≤ U : Cm and |LU/U | = d, then
d | m and
                             L ≤ LU = U : Cd = Hd .
The result follows.                                                            □
Lemma 3.4. Let p ≥ 17 be prime and let G = PSL2 (p). Every coset action G/H,
where H is contained in a torus normalizer or in a subgroup isomorphic to A4 , S4 ,
or A5 , has a base of size at most two, except possibly when p = 19 and H ∼
                                                                          = A5 .
Proof. It suffices to find, for each subgroup L listed above, some g ∈ G such that
L ∩ Lg = 1.
   A split torus normalizer is the stabilizer of an unordered pair {a, b} in P1 (Fp ).
The stabilizers of {a, b} and {a, c}, where a, b, c are distinct, have trivial intersection.
   Now let N be a nonsplit torus normalizer. By [16, Lemmas A.2 and A.3], |N | =
p + 1 and N has p(p − 1)/2 conjugates. A noninvolution of N determines its unique
nonsplit torus, so two distinct conjugates of N can intersect only in involutions.
Counting conjugates through the involutions of N gives at most
                         (p − 1)2
                                  when p ≡ 1          (mod 4)
                            4
conjugates meeting N , and at most
                          p2 + 4p + 7
                                         when p ≡ 3 (mod 4).
                                4
Both numbers are less than p(p − 1)/2 for p > 7. Hence N ∩ N g = 1 for some
g ∈ G.
   Finally, let E ∼
                  = A4 , S4 , or A5 . If E ∩ E g ̸= 1, then E ∩ E g contains a subgroup
of prime order. For a G-conjugacy class C of prime-order subgroups, let nC be the
number of its members contained in E. For g chosen uniformly at random in G, a
union bound gives
                                                    X n2
                                                           C
                               Pr(E ∩ E g ̸= 1) ≤            .
                                                         |C|
                                                     C
Every such class has at least p(p − 1)/2 members by [16, Lemmas A.2 and A.3].
The sums of the relevant numerators are 25, 97, 361 for A4 , S4 , and A5 , respectively.
Thus the probability is less than one for A4 and S4 when p ≥ 17, and for A5 when
p ≥ 29.
   By [16, Theorem A.1], among the primes 17 ≤ p < 29, an A5 subgroup occurs
only when p = 19. If H < A5 , then H is contained in an A4 or in a torus normalizer.
Thus only the action with p = 19 and H ∼  = A5 remains.                               □
Proposition 3.5. For d, e | m, the diagonal action of G on G/Hd ⊔ G/He is
3-closed.
Proof. Let Ed ≤ F×
                 p have order 2d. Then −1 ∈ Ed , and

                             G/Hd ∼
                                  = Xd = (F2p \ {0})/Ed .
Let πd : Xd −→ P1 (Fp ) be the natural projection.
           TOTAL 3-CLOSURE FOR PROJECTIVE SPECIAL LINEAR GROUPS                       7


   Take σ ∈ G(3),Xd ⊔Xe . By [14, Lemma 2.1], σ preserves both constituents and
every G-orbit on ordered pairs. For x = [v] ∈ Xd and y = [w] ∈ Xe , one has
                       πd (x) = πe (y)       ⇐⇒        det(v, w) = 0.
Hence σ induces the same permutation τ of P1 (Fp ) on both constituents.
  For three distinct projective points Li = ⟨vi ⟩, the square class
                   det(v1 , v2 ) det(v2 , v3 ) det(v3 , v1 )   mod (F×
                                                                     p)
                                                                        2


is well defined and G-invariant. Thus τ preserves this square class. After composing
with an element of G, we may assume that τ fixes ∞, 0, and 1. Its restriction f to
Fp then satisfies
                                  f (a) − f (b)
                                                ∈ (F×
                                                    p)
                                                       2
                                      a−b
for all a ̸= b. By Carlitz’s theorem [9, Theorem, p. 456], f is affine. Since f (0) = 0
and f (1) = 1, we have f = 1. Therefore τ ∈ G. Composing σ with an element of
G, we may assume that τ = 1.
   Fix r ∈ {d, e}. Since σ fixes every projective fiber, its action on the fiber over
L is multiplication by some cr,L ∈ F×    p /Er . For distinct lines L and M , the class
of det(v, w) modulo Er determines the G-orbit of the corresponding pair. Hence
cr,L cr,M = 1. Using three distinct lines, all cr,L are equal to some cr with c2r = 1.
   Choose points of Xr lying over three distinct projective points. By the definition
of the 3-closure, some g ∈ G agrees with σ on these three points. Since g fixes the
corresponding projective points, g = 1 [12, p. 245]. Hence cr = 1, and σ fixes Xr
pointwise. Applying this for r = d, e, we obtain σ = 1 after normalization. Thus
the original permutation belongs to G.                                               □
Theorem 3.6. For every prime p ≥ 17 with p ̸= 19, the group PSL2 (p) is totally
3-closed.
Proof. Let H, K < G. By Lemma 3.3, each of H and K is either conjugate to some
Hd , or its coset action has base size at most two by Lemma 3.4. Indeed, a subgroup
of a Borel subgroup which does not contain U is conjugate to a subgroup of the
split torus.
   By Lemma 2.3, every coset action with base size at most two is 3-closed. More-
over, Proposition 3.5, applied with d = e, implies that each action on G/Hd is
3-closed.
   If both H and K are conjugate to subgroups of the form Hd , then the action on
G/H ⊔G/K is 3-closed by Proposition 3.5. Otherwise, one constituent has base size
at most two, so the action is 3-closed by Proposition 2.4. The result now follows
from Proposition 2.2.                                                             □
3.2. The remaining four primes. It remains to treat the cases p = 7, 11, 13, 19.
The four proofs are similar and rely on the subgroup structure of each group,
particularly its maximal and nonmaximal subgroups. We begin with p = 7.
Theorem 3.7. The group PSL2 (7) is totally 3-closed.
Proof. Put G = PSL2 (7). The maximal subgroups of G consist of two conjugacy
classes of subgroups isomorphic to S4 and one conjugacy class of subgroups isomor-
phic to C7 ⋊ C3 [11, p. 3]. Thus the maximal coset actions are the point and line
actions on the Fano plane and the natural action on P1 (F7 ).
8              TING GONG, YONG YANG, AND MICHAEL RUOFAN ZENG


    The proper nonmaximal subgroups have types
                         C2 , C3 , C4 , C7 , V4 , S3 , D8 , A4 .
A direct count in the subgroup lattice shows that each has a conjugate with trivial
intersection. Hence every nonmaximal coset action has base size at most two, and
is therefore 3-closed by Lemma 2.3.
    Identify G ∼= GL3 (2) [8, Section 4, pp. 729–731]. In the point action on the
Fano plane, the two orbits on ordered triples of distinct points are the collinear and
noncollinear triples. Thus every element of the 3-closure preserves collinearity, and
hence belongs to the full automorphism group of the Fano plane, which is G. The
point action is therefore 3-closed, and the same holds for the line action by duality.
    Now consider the action on Ω = P1 (F7 ). Its two orbits on ordered triples of
distinct points are distinguished by the determinant square class. Let σ ∈ G(3),Ω .
After composing with an element of G, we may assume that σ fixes ∞, 0, 1. For
x ∈ F7 \{0, 1}, the triple orbits determine χ(x), χ(x−1) , where χ is the quadratic
character of F7 . These values fix 2, 4, and 6, leaving only the possible interchange
of 3 and 5. Indeed, ∆(∞, 2, x) = x − 2. Since 1 is a square and 3 is a nonsquare
in F7 , the triples (∞, 2, 3) and (∞, 2, 5) lie in different G-orbits. Hence σ cannot
interchange 3 and 5. Thus σ = 1 after normalization, and the degree-eight action
is 3-closed.
    It remains to consider diagonal actions on unions of two maximal coset actions.
If |H| = |K| = 24, then G ̸= HK, since |H||K|    |G|    = 24
                                                           7 ∈/ Z. Similarly, if |H| =
|K| = 21, then |H||K| |G|  = 218 ∈/ Z, so again G ̸= HK. Hence every union of two
degree-seven actions, as well as the union of two degree-eight actions, is 3-closed
by Proposition 2.5.
   Let X be the point set of the Fano plane and let Y = P1 (F7 ). Suppose that
σ ∈ G(3),X⊔Y . Since both constituent actions are 3-closed, after composing with
an element of G, we may assume that σ fixes X pointwise and acts on Y as some
g ∈ G. For distinct a, b ∈ X, the mixed triples (a, b, y) show that y g ∈ y Ga,b for
every y ∈ Y . Here Ga,b ∼   = V4 , and the seven such subgroups, indexed by the lines
of the Fano plane, each have two orbits of size four on Y . Under a suitable labeling
of Y = {∞, 0, . . . , 6}, the orbits containing ∞ are
              {∞, 0, 2, 6},   {∞, 1, 2, 4},   {∞, 2, 3, 5},   {∞, 0, 1, 3},
                     {∞, 0, 4, 5},   {∞, 1, 5, 6},    {∞, 3, 4, 6}.
The membership vectors of the eight points in these seven sets are distinct. Thus
a permutation preserving every one of these sets is trivial, so g = 1. The same
argument applies to the line action by duality.
   Therefore the diagonal action on every pair of maximal coset actions is 3-closed.
Combining this with Proposition 2.4 for nonmaximal stabilizers, the result follows
from Proposition 2.2.                                                             □

Theorem 3.8. The group PSL2 (11) is totally 3-closed.
Proof. Put G = PSL2 (11). The maximal subgroups of G are two conjugacy classes
of subgroups isomorphic to A5 , one class of subgroups isomorphic to C11 ⋊ C5 , and
one class of subgroups isomorphic to D12 [11]. A direct intersection calculation
shows that every coset action other than the two actions of degree eleven and the
           TOTAL 3-CLOSURE FOR PROJECTIVE SPECIAL LINEAR GROUPS                        9


action of degree twelve has a base of size at most two. Such actions are 3-closed by
Lemma 2.3.
    The two degree-eleven actions are the point and block actions of the unique 2-
(11, 5, 2) biplane, whose full automorphism group is G [3, Section 3, p. 5]. Let R
be the relation on triples of distinct points defined by requiring the three points to
lie in a block. We claim that the blocks are exactly the five-subsets all of whose
triples lie in R.
    Indeed, distinct blocks meet in two points. Let C be such a five-subset, choose
three points of C, and let B be the unique block containing them. If |B ∩ C| = 4,
the six unordered pairs in B ∩ C give six distinct blocks through the remaining
point of C, whereas each point lies in only five blocks. If |B ∩ C| = 3, the unique
second blocks through the three pairs in B ∩ C all contain the other two points of
C, contradicting the fact that two points lie in exactly two blocks. Hence C = B.
    Thus every element of the 3-closure preserves the blocks, and hence belongs to
G. The point action is 3-closed, and the block action is 3-closed by duality.
    Now consider the natural action of G on P1 (F11 ), and let σ lie in its 3-closure.
After composing with an element of G, we may assume that σ fixes ∞. For a ̸= b
in F11 , the G-orbit of (∞, a, b) is determined by the square class of b − a. Hence
                      b − a ∈ (F×
                                11 )
                                    2
                                        ⇐⇒     bσ − aσ ∈ (F×   2
                                                           11 ) .

Therefore σ|F11 is an automorphism of the Paley tournament on F11 . The auto-

                      x 7−→ ux + v,       u ∈ (F×   2
                                                11 ) ,   v ∈ F11 ,
by [17, Section 9.7]. This is precisely the stabilizer of ∞ in G, so the projective-line
action is 3-closed.
   It remains to consider the diagonal actions on unions of these three coset actions.
If H, K ∼= A5 , then
                               |H||K|     602     60
                                       =       =      ∈
                                                      / Z,
                                 |G|      660     11
so G ̸= HK. Similarly, if |H| = |K| = 55, then

and again G ̸= HK. Hence the diagonal action on any union of two degree-

Proposition 2.5.
   Let X = G/A5 , and let Y = P1 (F11 ). Take σ ∈ G(3),X⊔Y . Since both constituent
actions are 3-closed, we may normalize so that σ fixes X pointwise and its restriction
to Y is induced by some h ∈ G.
   For each x ∈ X, choose a subgroup P ≤ Gx of order 5. Then P = Gy,z for some
distinct y, z ∈ Y . Applying the definition of the 3-closure to (x, y, z) gives a ∈ Gx
                                           ah−1 ∈ Gy,z = P ≤ Gx , and hence h ∈ Gx .
such that y a = y h , and z a = z h . Thus T
Since this holds for every x ∈ X, h ∈ x∈X Gx = 1. Therefore the mixed action
on X ⊔ Y is 3-closed.
   Every pair of coset actions is now 3-closed by Proposition 2.4, Proposition 2.5,
or the preceding argument. The result follows from Proposition 2.2.                  □
Theorem 3.9. The group PSL2 (13) is totally 3-closed.
10              TING GONG, YONG YANG, AND MICHAEL RUOFAN ZENG


Proof. Put G = PSL2 (13). By Dickson’s classification [16, Theorem A.1], the
maximal proper subgroups of G are
                         C13 ⋊ C6 ,      D12 ,      D14 ,     A4 .
   The coset actions corresponding to D12 and D14 have bases of size two. For A4 ,
there are 91 conjugates, and at most 18 of them meet A4 nontrivially. Hence the
action on G/A4 also has a base of size two. The same holds for every subgroup
contained in one of these groups.
   Let U ∼= C13 and, for d | 6, put Hd = U ⋊ Cd . The action on G/H1 has a base
of size two. It remains to consider the actions corresponding to H2 , H3 , and H6 .
   The action on G/H6 ∼   = P1 (F13 ) is 3-closed. Indeed, after fixing ∞, the orbits
of the triples (∞, a, b) determine whether b − a is a square. Thus a normalized
element of the 3-closure induces an automorphism of the Paley graph on F13 . Its
automorphism group consists of the maps
                        x 7−→ ux + v,       u ∈ (F×   2
                                                  13 ) ,    v ∈ F13
[17, Theorem 9.1]. This is precisely the stabilizer of ∞ in G.
   Now let E ≤ F×                                                   2
                         13 have order 4 or 6, and write XE = (F13 \ {0})/E. These are
                                                             (3),XE
the actions corresponding to H2 and H3 . Let σ ∈ G                  . Since det(v, w) = 0 if
and only if [v] and [w] lie over the same point of P1 (F13 ), the pair orbits recover
the natural projection XE −→ P1 (F13 ). The induced permutation of the projective
line belongs to G by the preceding argument, so we may normalize it to be trivial.
   The restriction of σ to the fiber over a line L is then multiplication by some
cL ∈ F×   13 /E. For distinct lines L and M , preservation of the determinant class
gives cL cM = 1. Using three distinct lines, all cL are equal to some c with c2 = 1.
   If |E| = 4, then F×      13 /E has order 3, so c = 1. If |E| = 6, suppose that c is the
nontrivial element of F×       13 /E. Applying the definition of the 3-closure to the triple
([e1 ], [e2 ], [e1 + e2 ]) yields an element of G which agrees with σ on this triple and
therefore fixes the three corresponding projective points. Such an element is trivial,
and hence cannot induce the nontrivial scalar class c. Thus c = 1 in this case as
well, and both actions are 3-closed.
   Every remaining pair of coset actions either contains an action with a base of
size at most two, in which case Proposition 2.4 applies, or has stabilizers among
H2 , H3 , H6 . No two of these subgroups factorize G, so Proposition 2.5 applies. The
result follows from Proposition 2.2.                                                      □
Theorem 3.10. The group PSL2 (19) is totally 3-closed.
Proof. Put G = PSL2 (19), let U ∼    = C19 , and set Hd = U ⋊ Cd for d | 9. By
Lemmas 3.3 and 3.4, every proper subgroup of G is either conjugate to some Hd ,
contained in a subgroup whose coset action has a base of size at most two, or
isomorphic to A5 . The first two types are covered by Proposition 3.5 and by
Lemma 2.3 together with Proposition 2.4.
   There are two conjugacy classes of A5 subgroups, each giving a degree-57 coset
action. It remains to show that these two actions are 3-closed and to consider their
unions with the actions on G/H3 and G/H9 . The action on G/H1 has a base of
size two and is already covered by Proposition 2.4.
   Let X be the coset space corresponding to either conjugacy class of A5 subgroups.
Join two points of X when their stabilizers intersect in a subgroup isomorphic to
D10 . The resulting graph Γ is the Perkel graph [23, pp. 163–165]. It has intersection
           TOTAL 3-CLOSURE FOR PROJECTIVE SPECIAL LINEAR GROUPS                     11


array {6, 5, 2; 1, 1, 3} and full automorphism group G [4, Section 5.8.5, pp. 70–71].
The edge set of Γ is a union of G-orbits on pairs, so G(2),X ≤ Aut(Γ) = G. Both
degree-57 actions are therefore 2-closed, and hence 3-closed.
   The diagonal action on any two degree-57 actions is 3-closed by Proposition 2.5.
Indeed, if A, B ∼ = A5 , then
                              |A||B|    602   20
                                     =      =    ∈
                                                 / Z,
                                |G|    3420   19
so G ̸= AB.
   If one of the two coset actions has a base of size at most two, then their diagonal
action is 3-closed by Proposition 2.4. This applies in particular to the action on
G/H1 , where H1 ∼  = C19 , since two distinct Sylow 19-subgroups intersect trivially.
   It remains to pair an A5 action X with Y = G/Hd , where d = 3 or 9. Both
actions are 3-closed. Let σ ∈ G(3),X⊔Y . After composing with an element of G, we
may assume that σ fixes Y pointwise and that its restriction to X is induced by
some h ∈ G.
   The subdegrees of the degree-57 action are 1, 6, 20, 30, and the two-point sta-
bilizers on the suborbit of length 20 have order 3 [23, pp. 163–165]. Thus every
subgroup of order 3 in G is the stabilizer of two points of X.
   For y ∈ Y , choose P ≤ Gy of order 3 and points x1 , x2 ∈ X such that Gx1 ,x2 = P .
Applying the definition of the 3-closure to (x1 , x2 , y) gives a ∈ G such that
                         xa1 = xh1 ,   xa2 = xh2 ,   y a = y.
Hence a ∈ Gy and
                              ah−1 ∈ Gx1 ,x2 = P ≤ Gy ,
so h ∈ Gy . Since this holds for every y ∈ Y and the action on Y is faithful, h = 1.
Therefore the action on X ⊔ Y is 3-closed.
   The pairs of actions on G/Hd ⊔ G/He are handled by Proposition 3.5. Hence
every two-constituent coset action is 3-closed, and the result follows from Proposi-
tion 2.2.                                                                         □

  Combining the previous results, we obtain part (1) of Theorem 1.1.
Theorem 3.11. Let G = PSL2 (q) be a finite nonabelian simple group. Then G is
totally 3-closed if and only if q ≥ 7 is a prime.
Proof. Theorems 3.6, 3.7, 3.8, 3.9, and 3.10 show that PSL2 (p) is totally 3-closed
for every prime p ≥ 7. Proposition 3.1 excludes every proper prime power, while
Proposition 3.2 excludes q = 5. Finally, PSL2 (2) and PSL2 (3) are not nonabelian
simple.                                                                           □

                         4. The PSL3 (q) classification
   In this section, we prove that PSL3 (q) is totally 3-closed when q = 3 and when
q is a prime with q ≡ 2 (mod 3). The converse direction is proved in Section 5.

4.1. The case q = 3. We begin with q = 3 and put G = PSL3 (3). Since
|Z(SL3 (3))| = gcd(3, 3 − 1) = 1, we have G = SL3 (3). Moreover, |G| = 33 (32 −
1)(33 − 1) = 5616 = 24 · 33 · 13, and G is nonabelian simple [11]. We first record
the maximal subgroups of G.
12               TING GONG, YONG YANG, AND MICHAEL RUOFAN ZENG


Lemma 4.1. Up to conjugacy, the maximal subgroups of G are
               P,     P ∗,     J∼= C13 ⋊ C3 ,    M∼ = S4 ,
where P and P ∗ are respectively a point stabilizer and a line stabilizer in PG(2, 3).
Their orders and indices are
                             H       P    P∗      J    M
                            |H|     432 432 39 24
                          [G : H] 13 13 144 234
Proof. The maximal subgroups of G consist of two conjugacy classes of subgroups
of type 32 :2S4 , one class of type 13:3, and one class of type S4 [25]. The two
subgroups of order 432 are respectively the point and line stabilizers in PG(2, 3).
The displayed orders and indices now follow from |G| = 5616.                     □
     We first treat the J and M cases by counting conjugates.
Lemma 4.2. If H is contained in a conjugate of J or M , then the action of G on
G/H has a base of size at most two.
Proof. It suffices to find g ∈ G such that
                        J ∩ Jg = 1     and      M ∩ M g = 1.
   There are 144 conjugates of J. Let R ∼  = C13 be its normal Sylow 13-subgroup.
Every nonidentity element of R lies in a unique conjugate of J, since NG (R) = J.
The other 26 elements of J have order 3 and lie in a conjugacy class of size 624 [7,
table L3(3) and the fusion from 13:3]. Hence each lies in 144·26
                                                              624 = 6 conjugates of
J. Therefore at most 26(6 − 1) = 130 < 143 other conjugates meet J nontrivially.
Thus J ∩ J g = 1 for some g ∈ G.
   There are 234 conjugates of M . The group M ∼     = S4 contains nine involutions
and eight elements of order 3. These lie in conjugacy classes of sizes 117 and
624, respectively [7, table L3(3) and the fusion from s4]. Thus an involution lies in
234·9                                                           234·8
 117 = 18 conjugates of M , while an element of order 3 lies in 624 = 3 conjugates.
Every nontrivial subgroup of S4 contains an element of order 2 or 3, so at most
9(18 − 1) + 8(3 − 1) = 169 < 233 other conjugates meet M nontrivially. Hence
M ∩ M g = 1 for some g ∈ G.
   Finally, if H ≤ J or H ≤ M , the same choice of g gives H ∩ H g = 1. Therefore
the action on G/H has a base of size at most two.                                  □
     We next treat the point and line actions.
Lemma 4.3. The natural actions of G on the points and lines of PG(2, 3) are
3-closed.
Proof. Consider first the action on points. Two ordered triples of pairwise distinct
points lie in the same G-orbit if and only if they are either both collinear or both
noncollinear. Since G is 2-transitive, the G-orbits on triples with at most two
distinct entries are determined by which coordinates are equal.
   Thus every element of the 3-closure preserves collinearity, and hence acts on
PG(2, 3) as a collineation. By the fundamental theorem of projective geometry,
every collineation is induced by a semilinear transformation [6, Theorem 1.9.1].
Since Aut(F3 ) = 1 and PGL3 (3) = PSL3 (3) = G, the point action is 3-closed. The
same argument applied to the dual projective plane proves that the line action is
3-closed.                                                                         □
           TOTAL 3-CLOSURE FOR PROJECTIVE SPECIAL LINEAR GROUPS                   13


   It remains to treat the subgroups of P and P ∗ whose coset actions do not have
a base of size two. Fix a point stabilizer P and put
                 E(P ) = {H < P : H ∩ H g ̸= 1 for every g ∈ G}.
Thus H < P lies outside E(P ) if and only if the action on G/H has a base of size
at most two.
Proposition 4.4. The set E(P ) contains exactly twenty-four subgroups, forming
six G-conjugacy classes represented by subgroups of orders
                  48,      54,     72,      108,       144,      216.
Each corresponding coset action is 3-closed. The same holds for the six dual classes
contained in a line stabilizer.
Proof. This proposition is established by an exhaustive computation in GAP [22],
the only such computation in the paper. The complete program is reproduced,
together with its output, in Appendix A. The program constructs G in its degree-
13 point action and enumerates all 646 subgroups of P by cyclic extension.
   For each of the 645 proper subgroups H < P , the program tests one representa-
tive of every double coset in H\G/H. Since |H ∩ H g | is constant as g ranges over a
double coset HgH, this test is exhaustive. Of these subgroups, 621 have a conjugate
intersecting H trivially. Conjugacy tests in G show that the remaining twenty-four
form six G-conjugacy classes, one for each of the orders in the statement.
   Let Ω = G/H, let x = H ∈ Ω be the point corresponding to the trivial coset,
and let Ax be the group of permutations of Ω that fix x and preserve every Gx -
orbit on Ω × Ω. Every element of G(3),Ω fixing x preserves each G-orbit of triples
with first entry x, and therefore lies in Ax . The program determines Ax by exact
backtracking and then removes every element that fails to preserve some G-orbit
on Ω3 :
                          |H|             48 54 72 108 144 216
             #{K ∈ E(P ) : |K| = |H|}      9 4 3          4     3      1
                         |Ax |            48 54 72 108 288 1944
                      |(G(3),Ω )x |       48 54 72 108 144 216
For the first four classes, we already have Ax = Gx = H. For the final two classes,
the group Ax is larger, but every element of Ax \ Gx fails to preserve some G-orbit
on Ω3 . Hence (G(3),Ω )x = H in all six cases.
   Since G ≤ G(3),Ω , the group G(3),Ω is transitive. Therefore
                   |G(3),Ω | = |Ω| |(G(3),Ω )x | = |G : H| |H| = |G|.
Thus G(3),Ω = G.
   Finally, the automorphism g 7→ (g −1 )T interchanges point and line stabilizers,
giving the six dual classes.                                                     □
  We now turn to diagonal actions on two coset spaces.
Lemma 4.5. Let Ω1 and Ω2 be faithful transitive 3-closed G-sets. Suppose that
there are surjective G-maps ρi : Ωi −→ Yi , where each Yi is either the point set or
the line set of PG(2, 3). Then the diagonal action of G on Ω1 ⊔ Ω2 is 3-closed.
Proof. Let σ ∈ G(3),Ω1 ⊔Ω2 . By [14, Lemma 2.2], its restrictions to Ω1 and Ω2
lie in the corresponding 3-closures. Thus they are induced by elements a, b ∈ G.
14             TING GONG, YONG YANG, AND MICHAEL RUOFAN ZENG


After composing with the diagonal action of a−1 , we may assume that σ fixes Ω1
pointwise and acts on Ω2 as some t ∈ G.
   By [14, Lemma 2.1], σ preserves every G-orbit on Ω1 × Ω2 . If Y1 and Y2 are of
the same type, apply this to the G-invariant relation ρ1 (x) = ρ2 (y). Since ρ1 and
ρ2 are surjective, it follows that t fixes every point of Y2 .
   If Y1 and Y2 are of opposite types, consider the G-invariant relation defined by
requiring the point ρ1 (x) to lie on the line ρ2 (y), or vice versa. Since σ fixes Ω1
pointwise, it follows that t preserves every point-line incidence involving an element
of Y1 . Surjectivity of ρ1 and ρ2 then implies that t fixes every element of Y2 .
   The point and line actions of G are faithful, so t = 1. Hence σ is induced by an
element of G, and the diagonal action is 3-closed.                                  □

Theorem 4.6. The group G = PSL3 (3) is totally 3-closed.
Proof. Let H, K < G be proper subgroups. By Lemma 4.1, each is contained in a
conjugate of P , P ∗ , J, or M .
   If H is contained in a conjugate of J or M , then the action on G/H has a base
of size at most two by Lemma 4.2. The same holds if H is contained in a conjugate
of P or P ∗ but does not belong to one of the exceptional classes in Proposition 4.4.
Otherwise, the action on G/H is the point action, the line action, or one of the
exceptional parabolic actions. These actions are 3-closed by Lemmas 2.3 and 4.3
and Proposition 4.4. The same conclusions hold for K.
   If either action has a base of size at most two, then the diagonal action on
G/H ⊔G/K is 3-closed by Proposition 2.4. Otherwise, both actions admit surjective
G-maps onto the point set or the line set of PG(2, 3), so Lemma 4.5 applies.
   Thus the diagonal action on G/H ⊔ G/K is 3-closed for every pair of proper
subgroups H, K < G. The result follows from Proposition 2.2.                       □

4.2. The primes p ≡ 2 (mod 3). In this subsection, we prove that if p is a prime
with p ≡ 2 (mod 3), then PSL3 (p) is totally 3-closed. The remaining prime power
cases are treated together with higher ranks in Section 5.
   For p = 2, the result follows from PSL3 (2) ∼   = PSL2 (7) and Theorem 3.7.
Throughout the remainder of this subsection, p denotes a prime with p ≥ 5 and
p ≡ 2 (mod 3). Since |Z(SL3 (p))| = gcd(3, p − 1) = 1, we have G = PSL3 (p) =
SL3 (p).
   We begin with a rigidity statement for the scalar-fiber actions.
Proposition 4.7. Let p ≥ 5 be a prime with p ≡ 2 (mod 3), let G = PSL3 (p) =
SL3 (p), and let C ≤ F×
                      p . Put

                                ΩC = (F3p \ {0})/C.
Then the natural action of G on ΩC is faithful and 3-closed.
Proof. Let g lie in the kernel of the action. Then g fixes every point of P2 (Fp ), so
g is scalar. Since det(g) = 1 and gcd(3, p − 1) = 1, it follows that g = 1. Thus the
action is faithful.
   Let π : ΩC −→ P2 (Fp ) be the natural map, and let σ ∈ G(3),ΩC . Two elements
of ΩC have the same image under π if and only if their representatives are linearly
dependent. Since σ preserves the G-orbits on ordered pairs, it preserves the fibers
of π and induces a permutation of P2 (Fp ).
           TOTAL 3-CLOSURE FOR PROJECTIVE SPECIAL LINEAR GROUPS                     15


   The induced permutation preserves collinearity, since three projective points
are collinear if and only if their representatives are linearly dependent. By the
fundamental theorem of projective geometry, it is induced by a semilinear trans-
formation [6, Theorem 1.9.1]. Since Fp has no nontrivial field automorphisms and
PGL3 (p) = PSL3 (p) = G, the induced permutation belongs to G. After composing
σ with the inverse of this element, we may assume that σ fixes every fiber of π
setwise.
   Choose a nonzero representative vL for each L ∈ P2 (Fp ), and put A = F× p /C.
The fiber over L is identified with A by a 7−→ [avL ]. Thus σ induces a bijection
fL : A → A on each fiber.
   Let L1 , L2 , L3 be noncollinear. The G-orbit of
                               ([a1 vL1 ], [a2 vL2 ], [a3 vL3 ])
is determined by a1 a2 a3 ∈ A. Hence
                         fL1 (a1 )fL2 (a2 )fL3 (a3 ) = a1 a2 a3 .
Varying one coordinate shows that fL (a) = uL a for some uL ∈ A. Moreover,
uL1 uL2 uL3 = 1 whenever L1 , L2 , L3 are noncollinear.
   Given L, L′ ∈ P2 (Fp ), choose distinct points M, N on a line containing neither
L nor L′ . Comparing the triples (L, M, N ) and (L′ , M, N ) gives uL = uL′ . Thus
all uL are equal to some u ∈ A, and u3 = 1. Since |A| | p − 1 and 3 ∤ p − 1, we have
u = 1. Therefore σ = 1 after composition, and the original permutation belongs to
G.                                                                                □
  Now we treat the nonparabolic maximal subgroups.
Proposition 4.8. Let H be contained in a nonparabolic maximal subgroup of G.
Then the action of G on G/H has a base of size at most two.
Proof. Let H ≤ M < G, where M is nonparabolic and maximal. It is enough to
find g ∈ G such that M ∩ M g = 1. Indeed, this then gives H ∩ H g = 1.
   By the subgroup classification for PSL3 (p) [20, Theorem 2.4], the subgroup M
is one of the following:
      (i) the stabilizer N2 of a projective triangle;
     (ii) the normalizer N3 of a Singer cycle;
    (iii) a subgroup isomorphic to SO3 (p);
    (iv) a subgroup isomorphic to PSL2 (7).
The other cases in the classification do not occur because p is prime and 3 ∤ p − 1.
   Suppose first that M = N2 . Let ∆ = {⟨e1 ⟩, ⟨e2 ⟩, ⟨e3 ⟩}, and put
              v1 = e1 + e2 ,      v2 = e2 + 2e3 ,           v3 = e1 + e2 + e3 .
The matrix                                       
                                        1 0 1
                                 g2 = 1 1 1
                                        0 2 1
has determinant one, and N2 stabilizes ∆′ = {⟨v1 ⟩, ⟨v2 ⟩, ⟨v3 ⟩}. Let x ∈ N2 ∩ N2g2 .
                            g2

Write x = DPτ , where D is diagonal and τ ∈ S3 . Since ⟨v3 ⟩ is the unique point
of ∆′ whose coordinates are all nonzero, x fixes ⟨v3 ⟩. Hence D is scalar. The only
coordinate permutations preserving the supports of ⟨v1 ⟩ and ⟨v2 ⟩ are 1 and (1 3),
while
                       (1 3)⟨v1 ⟩ = ⟨e2 + e3 ⟩ ̸= ⟨e2 + 2e3 ⟩.
16              TING GONG, YONG YANG, AND MICHAEL RUOFAN ZENG


Thus τ = 1, so x = dI. Since d3 = 1 and gcd(3, p − 1) = 1, we have x = 1.
Therefore N2 ∩ N2g2 = 1.
  Now suppose that M = N3 . Identify F3p with K = Fp3 and put
                           T = {x 7→ ax : NK/Fp (a) = 1}.
If σ : x 7→ xp , then N3 = T ⋊ ⟨σ⟩. Set n = p2 + p + 1, so |T | = n and |N3 | = 3n.
Since 3 ∤ n, every element of N3 \ T has order three.
   For 1 ̸= x ∈ T , one has
                       |CG (x)| = n       and         |xG ∩ N3 | = 3.
Thus
                    {g ∈ G : x ∈ N3g } = |xG ∩ N3 | |CG (x)| = 3n.
For y ∈ N3 \ T ,
                    |CG (y)| = p2 − 1         and         |y G ∩ N3 | = 2n,
so that
                       {g ∈ G : y ∈ N3g } = 2n(p2 − 1).
Summing over the n − 1 nontrivial elements of T and the 2n elements of N3 \ T
gives
              {g ∈ G : N3 ∩ N3g ̸= 1} ≤ 3n(n − 1) + 4n2 (p2 − 1).
Since |G| = p3 (p − 1)n(p2 − 1) and
       |G| − 3n(n − 1) − 4n2 (p2 − 1)
                                      = p6 − p5 − 5p4 − 3p3 − 3p2 + p + 4 > 0
                      n
for p ≥ 5, there exists g3 ∈ G such that N3 ∩ N3g3 = 1.
    Suppose next that M = SO(V, B) for a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form
B. Identify V with K = Fp3 . After an isometry, we may write B(x, y) =
TrK/Fp (cxy) for some c ∈ K × . Choose 1 ̸= α ∈ K × with NK/Fp (α) = 1, and
let A be multiplication by α. Then A is self-adjoint with respect to B and has
irreducible minimal polynomial of degree three.
    Define BA (x, y) = B(Ax, y). The forms B and BA have the same discriminant,
so there exists g ∈ G such that SO(BA ) = SO(B)g . If x ∈ SO(B) ∩ SO(BA ), then
xA = Ax. Hence x is multiplication by some β ∈ K × . Preservation of B gives
β 2 = 1, so x = ±I. Since x ∈ G and det(−I) = −1, we obtain x = I. Thus
SO(B) ∩ SO(B)g = 1.
    Finally, suppose that M ∼ = PSL2 (7). This case can occur only for p ≥ 11, so
p ∤ |M | and every nonidentity element of M is semisimple. The numbers of elements
of orders 2, 3, 4, and 7 in M are
                             21,        56,         42,      48.
Every noncentral semisimple element of G has centralizer of order at most p(p −
1)2 (p + 1). Therefore
          {g ∈ G : M ∩ M g ̸= 1} ≤ (212 + 562 + 422 + 482 )p(p − 1)2 (p + 1)
                                   = 7645p(p − 1)2 (p + 1).
Since 7645 < p2 (p2 + p + 1) for p ≥ 11, this number is smaller than |G| = p3 (p3 −
1)(p2 − 1). Hence M ∩ M g = 1 for some g ∈ G.
   Thus in every case there exists g ∈ G such that M ∩ M g = 1. It follows that
H ∩ H g = 1, so the action on G/H has a base of size at most two.                 □
           TOTAL 3-CLOSURE FOR PROJECTIVE SPECIAL LINEAR GROUPS                       17


  We next prove a lemma used in the treatment of the parabolic subgroups.
Lemma 4.9. Let p ≥ 5, let L = GL2 (p), and let M ≤ L with SL2 (p) ≰ M . If D
is a split maximal torus of L, then there exists g ∈ L such that
                              D ∩ M g = D ∩ coreL (M ).
Proof. Let Z = Z(L), let π : L −→ PGL2 (p), and put A = π(M ). We first claim
that A does not contain PSL2 (p). Otherwise,
                           π([M, M ]) = [A, A] ≥ PSL2 (p).
Since [M, M ] ≤ SL2 (p), the subgroup M ∩SL2 (p) maps onto PSL2 (p). It is therefore
either SL2 (p) or a subgroup of index two. The latter is impossible because SL2 (p)
is perfect, while the former contradicts the hypothesis.
   By the subgroup classification of PGL2 (p) [13, Theorem D], the group A is cyclic,
dihedral, elementary abelian of order four, isomorphic to A4 , S4 , or A5 , or contained
in an affine subgroup. We show that A has a base of size at most two on P1 (Fp ).
   An affine subgroup has the base (0, 1). A subgroup of a split torus normalizer has
the base (1, c) for any c ̸= 0, ±1. For a nonsplit torus normalizer, every nonidentity
torus element fixes no point of P1 (Fp ), while each element outside the torus fixes
at most two points. Since there are p + 1 such elements and 2(p + 1) < p(p + 1),
some ordered pair of distinct points has trivial stabilizer. A subgroup of order four
is contained in the centralizer of one of its involutions, which is a torus normalizer.
   Finally, let E ∼= A4 , S4 , or A5 . Every nonidentity element of PGL2 (p) fixes at
most two points, and hence at most two ordered pairs of distinct points. Thus E
has a base of size two whenever 2(|E|−1) < p(p+1). This holds for A4 when p ≥ 5,
for S4 when p ≥ 7, and for A5 when p ≥ 11. When p = 5, the case A5 = PSL2 (5)
is excluded. For S4 ≤ PGL2 (5), the transformations
                                                     z+2
                               a(z) = 2z,     b(z) =
                                                     z+3
generate a subgroup isomorphic to S4 . Its stabilizer of ∞ is ⟨a⟩, and no nonidentity
element of ⟨a⟩ fixes 1. Hence (∞, 1) is a base. Since PGL2 (5) has a unique conjugacy
class of S4 subgroups [13, Theorem D(7)], the claim follows.
   We now determine the core of M . The group corePGL2 (p) (A) is trivial. Indeed,
its intersection with the simple normal subgroup PSL2 (p) is trivial, and it there-
fore centralizes PSL2 (p). Since CPGL2 (p) (PSL2 (p)) = 1, the claim follows. Hence
coreL (M ) = M ∩ Z.
   Let (x, y) be a base for A on P1 (Fp ). Choose g ∈ L such that (x, y)g is the pair
of eigenlines of D. Then π(D) ∩ π(M g ) = 1, and therefore D ∩ M g ≤ Z. Since
M ∩ Z is central and Z ≤ D, we have M ∩ Z ≤ D ∩ M g . Consequently,
                  D ∩ M g = M ∩ Z = coreL (M ) = D ∩ coreL (M ).
                                                                                      □
  Now we are ready to prove the parabolic cases.
Lemma 4.10. Let P be a point or line stabilizer of G, and let H ≤ P . Then the
action of G on G/H is 3-closed.
Proof. By contragredient duality, it is enough to consider a point stabilizer. Put
         Ω = G/H,       Gb = G(3),Ω ,      P 0 = Q ⋊ SL2 (p),    Q∼ = F2 , p
18             TING GONG, YONG YANG, AND MICHAEL RUOFAN ZENG


and set J = HP 0 . Since P 0 ⊴ P , the subgroup J is well defined.
   The partition of Ω into the J-orbits is determined by a G-invariant relation on
ordered pairs. Hence Gb preserves this partition and induces a permutation group
on G/J. Moreover, this induced group is contained in the 3-closure of the action
of G on G/J.
   Let
                             C = J/P 0 ≤ P/P 0 ∼= F× .p

The action on G/J is isomorphic to the action on (F3p \ {0})/C. It is therefore
3-closed by Proposition 4.7. Thus, for c ∈ G,   b we may compose c with an element
of G and obtain k ∈ G fixing every J-orbit setwise.
                       b
    For each projective point x, let Xx be the corresponding J-orbit in Ω, let Px be
                                                                                     0
its stabilizer in G, and let Px0 be the corresponding conjugate of P 0 . Then αk ∈ αPx
for α ∈ Xx . Choose Hx ≤ Px corresponding to the action of Px on Xx , and put
Nx = corePx (Hx ).
    Write Px = Qx ⋊ Lx where Lx ∼      = GL2 (p). The action of Lx on Qx , written as
row vectors, is ρ(A)u = (det A)−1 uA−1 . The subgroup Nx ∩ Qx is Lx -invariant, so
it is either 1 or Qx .
    If Nx ∩ Qx = 1, then
                              [Nx , Qx ] ≤ Nx ∩ Qx = 1.
Thus Nx ≤ CPx (Qx ) = Qx , and hence Nx = 1.
   Suppose that Qx ≤ Nx . Then Nx /Qx is normal in Lx . Such a normal subgroup
either contains SL2 (p) or is scalar. Consequently, either Px0 ≤ Nx , or Nx = 1, or
Nx = Qx ⋊ Zx for some scalar subgroup Zx ≤ Lx . We say that Nx is small in the
latter two cases.
   If Nx and Ny are small and x ̸= y, then Nx ∩ Ny = 1. Indeed, taking x = ⟨e1 ⟩
and y = ⟨e2 ⟩, an element of the intersection has both forms
                        −2                              
                         c      u v            d   0     0
                        0      c 0 ,      u′ d−2 v ′  .
                           0    0 c            0   0     d

Equality gives c = d = c−2 and forces the off-diagonal entries to vanish. Thus
c3 = 1, so c = 1. Since the pairs (Px , Hx ) are G-conjugate, the same alternative
holds for every x.
   Suppose first that Nx is small for every x. Let F = (x, y, z) be an ordered
projective basis, and put

                     DF = Px ∩ Py ∩ Pz ,       Kx = DF ∩ Nx .

We claim that there exists ηx ∈ Xx such that (DF )ηx = Kx .
   Identify Px = Q ⋊ L, let M be the image of Hx in L, and put W = Hx ∩ Q. If
SL2 (p) ≤ M , then the smallness of Nx gives W = 0. Since −I acts as −1 on Q,
every complement to Q in Q ⋊ SL2 (p) is Q-conjugate to the standard complement.
We may therefore assume that Hx ≤ L.
   The two characters through which DF acts on Q have exponent matrix of de-
terminant 3. Since gcd(3, p − 1) = 1, the resulting map DF −→ (F×    2
                                                                  p ) is bijective.
A vector whose two coordinates are nonzero therefore gives a point ηx with trivial
DF -stabilizer.
            TOTAL 3-CLOSURE FOR PROJECTIVE SPECIAL LINEAR GROUPS                       19


    Now suppose that SL2 (p) ≰ M . By Lemma 4.9, after conjugating in L we may
assume that
                          DF ∩ M = DF ∩ coreL (M ) =: R.
If W = Q, the point corresponding to Hx has stabilizer DF ∩Hx = R = Kx . If W <
Q, then Nx = 1 and R is scalar. For 1 ̸= d = cI ∈ R, the map ρ(d) − 1 = (c−3 − 1)I
is invertible. The condition that d belong to a Q-conjugate of Hx excludes at most
one coset of W in Q. There are at most |R| − 1 ≤ p − 2 such excluded cosets,
whereas |Q/W | ≥ p. A conjugate outside their union gives the required point ηx .
    Choose such points ηx , ηy , ηz for the ordered basis F . Since k preserves their
G-orbit and fixes their three projective points, there exists tF ∈ DF such that
                             (ηx , ηy , ηz )k = (ηx , ηy , ηz )tF .
Set hF = kt−1F . Then hF fixes the three chosen points.
   Since G and G b have the same orbits on Ω3 , repeated application of [21, Theo-
rem 2.3(ii)] shows that Gηy ,ηz and G  b η ,η have the same orbits on Ω. Let u ∈ Xx .
                                          y z

There exists a ∈ Gηy ,ηz such that uhF = ua . Both points lie in Xx , so a fixes x.
Since a also fixes ηy and ηz , it fixes y and z. Hence
                  a ∈ DF ∩ Gηy ∩ Gηz = Ky ∩ Kz ≤ Ny ∩ Nz = 1.
Thus hF fixes Xx pointwise. By symmetry, it fixes Xy and Xz pointwise. Therefore
k and tF induce the same permutation on these three sets.
   If two ordered projective bases F and F ′ agree in two entries, then tF t−1  F ′ fixes
the corresponding two sets pointwise. Hence tF t−1F ′ ∈ N x ∩  N y =   1. The  graph   of
ordered projective bases, in which two bases are adjacent when they agree in two
entries, is connected. Thus all tF are equal to one element t ∈ G.
   Every projective point occurs in an ordered projective basis, and t fixes every
point in each such basis. Hence t fixes every point of P2 (Fp ). It is therefore scalar,
and so t = 1 because Z(G) = 1. The sets Xx cover Ω, so k = 1.
   Finally, suppose that Px0 ≤ Nx for every x. Since Px0 acts trivially on Xx , the
                  0
relation αk ∈ αPx implies αk = α for every α ∈ Xx . Again the sets Xx cover Ω, so
k = 1.
   Thus every element of G b belongs to G, and the action on G/H is 3-closed. □

  We now combine the preceding results.
Lemma 4.11. For every proper subgroup H < G, the action of G on G/H is 3-
closed. If H is contained in a nonparabolic maximal subgroup, then this action has
a base of size at most two.
Proof. Choose a maximal subgroup M of G containing H. If M is parabolic, then
the action on G/H is 3-closed by Lemma 4.10.
   If M is nonparabolic, then the action on G/H has a base of size at most two by
Proposition 4.8. It is therefore 3-closed by Lemma 2.3.                         □
Lemma 4.12. Let H ≤ PX and K ≤ PY , where PX and PY are point or line
parabolic subgroups of G. Then the diagonal action of G on G/H ⊔ G/K is 3-
closed.
Proof. By Lemma 4.10, the actions on G/H and G/K are 3-closed. There are
surjective G-maps
                  ρX : G/H −→ G/PX ,               ρY : G/K −→ G/PY ,
20             TING GONG, YONG YANG, AND MICHAEL RUOFAN ZENG


where G/PX and G/PY are respectively point or line sets of PG(2, p).
   Let π ∈ G(3),G/H⊔G/K . Constant triples show that π preserves each of the two
coset spaces. By [14, Lemma 2.2], its restrictions are induced by elements a, b ∈ G.
After composing π with a−1 , we may assume that π fixes G/H pointwise and acts
on G/K as δ = a−1 b ∈ G.
   Let x ∈ G/PX and y ∈ G/PY , and choose α ∈ ρ−1                    −1
                                                     X (x) and β ∈ ρY (y). By [14,
Lemma 2.1], there exists t ∈ G such that α = α and β = β . Hence xt = x and
                                             t            t    δ

yt = yδ .
   Suppose first that G/PX and G/PY are both point sets or both line sets. Since
equality is preserved by G, we have
                               x=y      ⇐⇒      x = yδ
for every x. Taking x = y gives y δ = y.
   Suppose now that one is the point set and the other is the line set. Since incidence
is preserved by G, for every point x and line y,
                               x∈y      ⇐⇒     x ∈ yδ .
A line is determined by its incident points, and a point is determined by its incident
lines. Thus again y δ = y.
   Therefore δ fixes every point or every line of PG(2, p). Since these actions of G
are faithful, δ = 1. Hence π is induced by the diagonal action of a ∈ G, and the
action on G/H ⊔ G/K is 3-closed.                                                    □

Theorem 4.13. Let p be a prime with p ≡ 2 (mod 3). Then PSL3 (p) is totally
3-closed.
Proof. For p = 2, the result follows from PSL3 (2) ∼
                                                   = PSL2 (7) and Theorem 3.7.
Assume that p ≥ 5.
   Let H, K < G be proper subgroups. By Lemma 4.11, the actions on G/H and
G/K are 3-closed. Choose maximal subgroups MH and MK containing H and K,
respectively.
   If either MH or MK is nonparabolic, then the corresponding coset action has a
base of size at most two by Lemma 4.11. Hence the diagonal action on G/H ⊔ G/K
is 3-closed by Proposition 2.4.
   If both MH and MK are parabolic, then the diagonal action is 3-closed by
Lemma 4.12.
   Thus the diagonal action on G/H ⊔ G/K is 3-closed for every pair of proper
subgroups H, K < G. The result follows from Proposition 2.2.                  □

        5. Negative results and the proof of the main theorem
   In this section, we establish the semilinear and central-vector obstructions and
complete the proof of Theorem 1.1. In particular, we prove that PSL4 (q) is not
totally 3-closed for any prime power q, and that PSLn (q) is not totally 3-closed
whenever n ≥ 5 and q > 2. This leaves only the family PSLn (2) with n ≥ 5.
Proposition 5.1. Let n ≥ 3, let q be a prime power, and let V = Fnq . Put
                  G = PSL(V ),       K = PGL(V ),         Ω = P(V ).
Then PΓL(V ) ≤ G(3),Ω .
            TOTAL 3-CLOSURE FOR PROJECTIVE SPECIAL LINEAR GROUPS                       21


Proof. Define δ : K −→ F×          × n                        × n
                              q /(Fq ) by δ([A]) = det(A)(Fq ) . This is well defined
and surjective, with kernel G.
   Let T = (L1 , L2 , L3 ) ∈ Ω3 , and let KT be its pointwise stabilizer in K. We claim
that δ(KT ) = F×        × n
                   q /(Fq ) . If the distinct lines in T span a subspace of dimension
at most two, scale a complementary basis vector by an arbitrary element of F×         q .
If L1 , L2 , L3 are independent, choose nonzero vi ∈ Li , extend them to a basis of
V , and scale v1 . In either case, the resulting element fixes T and has arbitrary
determinant class.
   Suppose that U = T k for some k ∈ K. Choose s ∈ KU such that δ(s) = δ(k)−1 .
Then ks ∈ G and T ks = U . Thus G and K have the same orbits on Ω3 .
   Two ordered triples lie in the same K-orbit if and only if the same coordinates
are equal and, when the three points are distinct, they are either both collinear or
both noncollinear. Every semilinear projectivity preserves these properties. Hence
every element of PΓL(V ) preserves every G-orbit on Ω3 , and therefore PΓL(V ) ≤
G(3),Ω .                                                                              □
Theorem 5.2. Let n ≥ 3 and let q = rf be a prime power. If f > 1 or
gcd(n, q − 1) > 1, then the natural action of PSLn (q) on Pn−1 (Fq ) is not 3-closed.
In particular, PSLn (q) is not totally 3-closed.
Proof. Put G = PSLn (q) and Ω = Pn−1 (Fq ). By Proposition 5.1, PΓLn (q) ≤
G(3),Ω .
  Suppose first that d = gcd(n, q − 1) > 1. Then [PGLn (q) : G] = d > 1. Since
                         G < PGLn (q) ≤ PΓLn (q) ≤ G(3),Ω ,
the action is not 3-closed.
   If f > 1, the Frobenius permutation
                            [x1 : · · · : xn ] 7−→ [xr1 : · · · : xrn ]
belongs to PΓLn (q) but not to PGLn (q). Thus in either case G < G(3),Ω , so the
action is not 3-closed.                                                       □
Theorem 5.3. Let n ≥ 4, let q > 2 be a prime power, let V = Fnq , and let
Z = Z(SL(V )). Put
             G = SL(V )/Z,          G
                                    e = GL(V )/Z,                Ω = (V \ {0})/Z.
Then the actions of G and G
                          e on Ω are faithful, and G e ≤ G(k),Ω for every 1 ≤ k < n.
                 ∼
In particular, G = PSLn (q) is not totally 3-closed.
Proof. Let A ∈ GL(V ) fix every Z-orbit in V \ {0}. For each 0 ̸= v ∈ V , write
Av = zv v for some zv ∈ Z. If u, v are linearly independent, then
                        zu u + zv v = A(u + v) = zu+v (u + v),
so zu = zv = zu+v . The same scalar occurs on every nonzero multiple of a vector.
Hence A = zI for some z ∈ Z. Thus the actions of G and G      e on Ω are faithful.
                                           ∼   ×
   Since Z ≤ SL(V ) and GL(V )/ SL(V ) = Fq , we have [G : G] = q − 1 > 1.
                                                            e
   Let 1 ≤ k < n, let A ∈ GL(V ), and consider (Zv1 , . . . , Zvk ) ∈ Ωk . Put
W = ⟨v1 , . . . , vk ⟩. Since dim W < n, choose a basis of V extending a basis of W .
There exists D ∈ GL(V ) which fixes W pointwise and satisfies det(D) = det(A)−1 .
Indeed, it is enough to scale one basis vector outside W . Then AD ∈ SL(V ), and
22               TING GONG, YONG YANG, AND MICHAEL RUOFAN ZENG


AD agrees with A on the given tuple. Hence every element of G    e can be matched
                                                         e≤G    (k),Ω
on every ordered k-tuple by an element of G. Therefore G              .
  Taking k = 3, we obtain G < G e ≤ G(3),Ω , so the action is not 3-closed.     □
Proposition 5.4. The group PSL4 (2) is not totally 3-closed.
Proof. Identify PSL4 (2) ∼      = A8 and let A8 act on the set Ω of two-subsets of
{1, . . . , 8} [11, p. 3]. This action is faithful.
   Let T = (X1 , X2 , X3 ) ∈ Ω3 . The union X1 ∪ X2 ∪ X3 contains at most six
points. Let s ∈ S8 and put U = T s . Choose two points outside the union of the
three entries of U , and let τ be the transposition of these two points. Then τ fixes
U pointwise. If s is odd, then sτ is even and
                                 T sτ = U τ = U = T s .
                                                                 (3),Ω
Hence every S8 -orbit on Ω3 is an A8 -orbit. Therefore S8 ≤ A8 . Since A8 < S8 ,
the action is not 3-closed. Thus PSL4 (2) is not totally 3-closed.           □
     We can now complete the classification.
Proof of Theorem 1.1. Part (1) is Theorem 3.11.
   For n = 3, the positive cases follow from Theorems 4.6 and 4.13. If q = rf with
f > 1, or if q is prime and q ≡ 1 (mod 3), the group is not totally 3-closed by
Theorem 5.2. This proves part (2).
   Suppose that n = 4. If q > 2, the result follows from Theorem 5.3. If q = 2, it
follows from Proposition 5.4. This proves part (3).
   Finally, if n ≥ 5 and q > 2, the result follows from Theorem 5.3. This proves
part (4). Hence only the cases PSLn (2) with n ≥ 5 remain.                      □

                       Appendix A. The GAP verification
   The following GAP program carries out the computation used in the proof of
Proposition 4.4. It constructs G = PSL3 (3) in its action on the thirteen points of
PG(2, 3), enumerates the 646 subgroups of the point stabilizer P , determines the
twenty-four exceptional subgroups and their six G-conjugacy classes, and computes
the groups Ax and (G(3),Ω )x for one representative of each class. The program was
executed under GAP 4.12.1 [22] and runs in under ten seconds.
         Listing 1. The verification program psl33 exceptional gap.txt.
 1    # psl33_exceptional.g
 2    #
 3    # Verification of the exceptional-subgroup classification for
 4    # G = PSL(3,3) = SL(3,3): enumerates all subgroups of a point
 5    # stabilizer P, determines the set E(P) of subgroups H < P with
 6    # H meeting every G-conjugate of itself, classifies E(P) up to
 7    # G-conjugacy, and verifies that each exceptional coset action
 8    # G/H is 3-closed.
 9    #
10    # Run as: gap -q -A -b psl33_exceptional.g
11
12    # G acting on the 13 points of PG(2,3), P = stabilizer of point 1.
13    pts := Set(Filtered(GF(3)^3, v -> not IsZero(v)), NormedRowVector);;
14    G := Image(ActionHomomorphism(SL(3,3), pts, OnLines));;
15    P := Stabilizer(G, 1);;
16    Print("|G| = ", Size(G), " |P| = ", Size(P), "\n");
17
            TOTAL 3-CLOSURE FOR PROJECTIVE SPECIAL LINEAR GROUPS            23


18   # All subgroups of P, by cyclic extension.
19   subs := Concatenation(List(ConjugacyClassesSubgroups(
20             LatticeByCyclicExtension(P)), AsList));;
21   Print("subgroups of P: ", Length(subs), "\n");
22
23   # |H meet H^g| is constant on the double coset HgH, so one
24   # representative per double coset is an exhaustive test.
25   IsExceptional := function(H)
26     local g;
27     if Size(H) = 1 or Size(H) = Size(P) then return false; fi;
28     for g in List(DoubleCosets(G, H, H), Representative) do
29       if IsTrivial(Intersection(H, H^g)) then return false; fi;
30     od;
31     return true;
32   end;;
33   exc := Filtered(subs, IsExceptional);;
34   Print("exceptional subgroups: ", Length(exc), "\n");
35   Print("order distribution: ", Collected(List(exc, Size)), "\n");
36
37   # G-conjugacy classes of the exceptional subgroups.
38   classes := [];;
39   for H in exc do
40     cl := First(classes, c -> Size(c[1]) = Size(H)
41                               and IsConjugate(G, c[1], H));
42     if cl = fail then Add(classes, [H, 1]);
43     else cl[2] := cl[2] + 1; fi;
44   od;
45   Print("classes [order, members in P]: ",
46         List(classes, c -> [Size(c[1]), c[2]]), "\n");
47
48   # For x = H in Omega = G/H, the group A_x of permutations of Omega
49   # fixing x and preserving every G_x-orbit on Omega^2 contains the
50   # stabilizer of x in G^(3). Backtracking enumerates A_x; the
51   # transported pair coloring then filters by the G-orbits on Omega^3:
52   # the G-orbit of (i,j,k) is determined by D[T_i(j)][T_i(k)], where
53   # T_i carries i back to x and D is the G_x-orbit coloring of pairs.
54   ClosureStabilizer := function(H)
55     local act, GG, N, stab, orb, D, ncol, rp, Ti, i, o,
56           A2, A3, img, used, search, pi, ok, j, k;
57     act := FactorCosetAction(G, H);
58     GG := Image(act);
59     N := Index(G, H);
60     stab := Stabilizer(GG, 1);
61     orb := OrbitsDomain(stab, Cartesian([1..N], [1..N]), OnPairs);
62     D := List([1..N], i -> []);
63     for i in [1..Length(orb)] do
64       for o in orb[i] do D[o[1]][o[2]] := i; od;
65     od;
66     ncol := Length(orb);
67     rp := List([1..N], i -> RepresentativeAction(GG, 1, i));
68     Ti := List([1..N], i -> List([1..N], j -> j^(rp[i]^-1)));
69     A2 := [];
70     img := [1];
71     used := BlistList([1..N], [1]);
72     search := function(v)
73       local w, a, good;
74       if v > N then Add(A2, PermList(ShallowCopy(img))); return; fi;
75       for w in [1..N] do
24                TING GONG, YONG YANG, AND MICHAEL RUOFAN ZENG


 76           if not used[w] then
 77             good := true;
 78             for a in [1..v-1] do
 79               if D[a][v] <> D[img[a]][w]
 80                   or D[v][a] <> D[w][img[a]] then
 81                 good := false; break;
 82               fi;
 83             od;
 84             if good then
 85               img[v] := w; used[w] := true;
 86               search(v+1);
 87               used[w] := false; Unbind(img[v]);
 88             fi;
 89           fi;
 90        od;
 91      end;
 92      search(2);
 93      if Length(A2) = Size(H) then
 94        A3 := A2;
 95      else
 96        A3 := [];
 97        for pi in A2 do
 98           ok := true;
 99           for i in [1..N] do
100             for j in [1..N] do
101               for k in [1..N] do
102                 if D[Ti[i][j]][Ti[i][k]]
103                     <> D[Ti[i^pi][j^pi]][Ti[i^pi][k^pi]] then
104                    ok := false; break;
105                 fi;
106               od;
107               if not ok then break; fi;
108             od;
109             if not ok then break; fi;
110           od;
111           if ok then Add(A3, pi); fi;
112        od;
113      fi;
114      return [Size(H), N, ncol, Length(A2), Length(A3),
115               Set(A3) = Set(Elements(stab))];
116    end;;
117
118    Print("[ |H|, |Omega|, pair colors, |A_x|, |3-closure stab|, ",
119          "= image of H ]\n");
120    for cl in classes do
121      Print(ClosureStabilizer(cl[1]), "\n");
122    od;
123    Print("total time (ms): ", Runtime(), "\n");
124    QUIT;

      The program produces the following output.
                             Listing 2. Output of Listing 1.
       |G| = 5616 |P| = 432
       subgroups of P: 646
       exceptional subgroups: 24
       order distribution: [ [ 48, 9 ], [ 54, 4 ], [ 72, 3 ], [ 108, 4 ],
         [ 144, 3 ], [ 216, 1 ] ]
             TOTAL 3-CLOSURE FOR PROJECTIVE SPECIAL LINEAR GROUPS                                25


    classes [order, members in P]: [ [ 48, 9 ], [ 54, 4 ], [ 72, 3 ], [ 108, 4 ],
      [ 144, 3 ], [ 216, 1 ] ]
    [ |H|, |Omega|, pair colors, |A_x|, |3-closure stab|, = image of H ]
    [ 48, 117, 345, 48, 48, true ]
    [ 54, 104, 264, 54, 54, true ]
    [ 72, 78, 148, 72, 72, true ]
    [ 108, 52, 72, 108, 108, true ]
    [ 144, 39, 22, 288, 144, true ]
    [ 216, 26, 16, 1944, 216, true ]
    total time (ms): 9482

    The six rows of the final output table match the table in the proof of Propo-
sition 4.4. In each exceptional class, the stabilizer of x in the 3-closure has order
|H| and coincides with the image of H. An independent implementation of the
same computation in Python, produced during the Albilich run that generated the
original argument, returns identical results.

and independently verified by the authors.
